overview: This record follows Nepal from the expanding Shah kingdom through Rana rule, struggles over democracy and the republic. Its 1783 start is an atlas snapshot, not Nepal’s founding date. Earlier Kathmandu Valley kingdoms have separate histories, and the changing map outline needs particular care.

sections.title: A kingdom, changing borders and governments

items.text: Prithvi Narayan Shah’s forces took Kathmandu in 1768 and defeated the three Malla kingdoms by 1769. Expansion joined previously separate states under the Gorkha dynasty. This was a process of conquest and political consolidation, not the beginning of the many communities and traditions living within Nepal.

The atlas draws Nepal far west into Garhwal already in 1783. That is premature: Gorkha dominion there followed the invasion of 1803. The repeated 1800 outline also compresses later expansion. Its contraction from 1815 broadly signals military defeat, but these snapshots do not establish precise yearly frontiers or resolve present boundary disputes.

War with the East India Company lasted from 1814 to 1816. British victory changed Nepal’s relationship with the growing colonial power in India. Recruitment of Nepalese soldiers into Company service began in 1815. Later Gurkha service is one strand of Nepal’s history; it should not make every Nepali person seem a soldier.

From 1846, the Rana family made the prime ministership hereditary and reduced Shah kings largely to ceremonial roles. Relatives controlled access to power. Rana government lasted until 1951, so a palace bearing a king’s name does not necessarily show who made the political decisions during this period.

After the democratic opening of 1951 and an elected government in 1959, King Mahendra took power in 1960. The 1962 constitution organized the partyless Panchayat system around royal authority. A popular movement restored multiparty democracy in 1990. Nepal’s political story repeatedly turned on who could participate and who could dismiss a government.

The Maoist insurgency began in 1996, and the ensuing war brought severe suffering and demands for social change. A peace agreement in 2006 opened another political transition. In May 2008 the monarchy was abolished. Ending a dynasty was a change in state institutions; Nepal’s people and country continued.

During his 1802 to 1803 visit, Francis Buchanan Hamilton described Newar brick houses with tiled roofs and carved wooden window screens. Architectural notes he included describe upper-floor benches overlooking the street. A window could let in air and light while giving a household a sheltered place to watch neighborhood life. These are an outside observer’s Kathmandu Valley examples.

Hamilton also described strong paper made at Bhaktapur from a shrub’s bark, useful for wrapping packages. He reported that local production did not meet demand and that paper and raw material also arrived from Tibet. Paper-making was part of a trading world, not an isolated craft locked inside one valley.

In Patan and Bhaktapur, Hamilton recorded workshops making copper, brass and bell-metal vessels for export to Tibet. Pots, lamps and other worked metal carried local skills beyond the valley. This early-nineteenth-century description reminds us that international trade could involve practical household objects as well as royal luxuries.

A familiar meal described by Nepal’s Tourism Board is dal, a lentil soup, with bhat, boiled rice, and tarkari, vegetables, often with achar or pickle. Other meals use roti or a thick cooked flour dish, and momos are popular dumplings. Regions and households vary: one plate cannot stand for everyone in the country.

During the Hindu festival Dashain, many families visit elders for blessings and tika, a forehead mark made with rice, yogurt and red color. The Tourism Board also describes new clothes, feasts, kite flying and village swings. A family reunion can include looking up at a kite as well as looking across a crowded table.

Tharu women interviewed in Lumbini in 2025 wove grasses into baskets for storing grain, carrying things and presenting wedding gifts. Panmati Tharuni recalled learning at twelve, leaving unfinished weaving to play and returning later. Her mother started the basket’s center for her. Learning a demanding craft could happen between ordinary childhood distractions.

In Mugu in 2019, community health volunteer Dev Laxmi Malla brought a handbook with pictures to a mothers’ group. Training helped her explain pregnancy and newborn services through discussion and role-play. Healthcare depended partly on trusted people making information understandable, not only on hospital buildings or equipment.

The same Mugu programme formed fathers’ groups to encourage men’s involvement in children’s wellbeing. It also collected expectant mothers’ phone numbers so information could arrive by text message. A family health system could connect a local meeting, a volunteer’s walk and a message on a phone.

Tilganga’s eye-care institute, inaugurated in 1994, became a WHO collaborating centre in 2019. Its work joined cataract treatment, specialist training, an eye bank and production of artificial lenses used inside the eye. Lenses made in Nepal were exported abroad. This was both medical care and precise manufacturing, with knowledge shared internationally.

UNICEF’s 2022 account of Bhanu Secondary School in Surkhet describes water storage and group handwashing facilities, five toilets each for girls and boys, and an accessible toilet. Students helped plan improvements. Sanitary pads and more suitable toilets reduced a practical worry for girls. The school had reached one star in its improvement scheme, with more work ahead.

Afsana Khatun returned to formal schooling after completing the nine-month SAGE programme in 2022. UNICEF’s 2024 story describes literacy and numeracy lessons using music, games and drama, alongside life skills. Facilitators helped her enroll at Shree Nepal Rashtriya Secondary School in Parsa. A second route into education mattered when her first route had broken down.

sections.title: Discoveries, technology and a written sample

items.text: After the 2015 earthquakes, archaeologists used ground-penetrating radar and excavations before rebuilding monuments. At Patan’s Char Narayan Temple they found an earlier timber-and-clay platform. Kasthamandap’s foundations proved undamaged despite the building’s collapse. These findings helped distinguish what needed replacement from what could still support reconstruction; the older remains are not inventions of the Shah period.

On 17 June 2019, NepaliSat-1 was released from the International Space Station’s Kibo module. Nepal’s Academy of Science and Technology and Japan’s Kyushu Institute of Technology developed it together. The BIRDS-3 project used CubeSats only ten centimeters along each side. A spacecraft could be small enough to fit between two hands.

The 2015 constitution organized Nepal as a federal democratic republic, with federal, provincial and local government. It recognized the country’s many languages and communities. A constitutional promise sets rules and goals; it does not by itself prove that every person receives equal treatment or that political disputes are finished.

The Nepali title “नेपालको संविधान”, transliterated “Nepālko saṃvidhān”, means “Constitution of Nepal”. It appears in the Law Commission’s text of the constitution promulgated on 20 September 2015. The sample uses Devanagari script. It is a modern written witness from Nepal, not an inscription surviving from the eighteenth-century kingdom.

Nepal’s constitutional flag description has two triangular shapes, a moon and a sun. Schedule 1 supplies a surprisingly elaborate construction method using lines, arcs and measurements. A flag can become a geometry exercise: drawing its shape correctly takes more thought than coloring a rectangle.

Political rights remained contested after the republic’s creation. In a communication dated January 2026, UN experts raised allegations of killings, detention and excessive force during the youth-led protests of September 2025. These were concerns requiring investigation, not final court findings. Constitutional government and accountability have continued to be matters people struggle over.

ending.text: Nepal continues as a country. The monarchy ended in 2008; the 2015 constitution set out a federal republic. Those political transformations did not end its communities, languages, household traditions or continuing debates about rights and representation.
